analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage from $4.25 to $4.75 an hour.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have raised the federal minimum wage by 50 cents an hour, was referred to a House committee and subcommittee in May 1995 and never received a vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the Fair Labor Standards Act, the federal law setting a wage floor, to raise the minimum wage from $4.25 to $4.75 an hour. The increase would take effect on the first day of the third month after the bill became law. It was introduced by a Republican representative with a handful of Democratic cosponsors, but it never left committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid at or near the federal minimum wage would see their hourly pay rise by 50 cents, to $4.75. That mostly means entry-level workers in retail, restaurants, and other service jobs.

how_it_helps.text: The bill raises the federal minimum wage from $4.25 to $4.75 an hour under the Fair Labor Standards Act [S2][S3].
The increase takes effect on the first day of the third month after enactment, so workers would see the raise within roughly a quarter of a year [S3].
A simple, single provision bill, it contains no phase-ins, carve-outs, or exemptions that would dilute the raise [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers who pay wages at or near the minimum, especially restaurants, retail stores, and other low-wage service businesses, would face higher payroll costs. Some of that cost is typically passed on through higher prices or reduced hiring at the bottom of the wage scale.

drawbacks.text: A 50-cent increase raises labor costs for businesses that employ many minimum-wage workers, such as restaurants and retail shops; opponents of minimum wage increases argue this can lead to fewer entry-level jobs or higher prices, particularly for small businesses [S3].

The proposed increase was modest relative to inflation, since the minimum wage had been stuck at $4.25 since 1991, so even if passed it would not have fully restored the wage floor's past purchasing power [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A straightforward, modest raise: about a 12% increase in the wage floor, phased in within three months, with the usual trade-off that low-wage employers bear higher payroll costs. The bill was narrow and clean, with no offsetting provisions either helping or burdening employers, so the costs and benefits fall where a reader would expect: workers gain, minimum-wage employers pay.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House committee that handles labor law in May 1995, then passed to a subcommittee that handles worker protections a week later, and it stayed there until the Congress ended — no committee vote, no floor vote, nothing.

narrative.text: Phil English, a Republican from Pennsylvania, introduced the bill on May 9, 1995 [S1][S3].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Economic and Educational Opportunities, the panel with jurisdiction over the Fair Labor Standards Act [S1][S5].
On May 19, 1995, it was referred to the subcommittee handling workforce protections, the last action the bill ever received [S5].
Three Democratic representatives cosponsored the bill, giving it small bipartisan support [S4].
No further action was taken before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, so the bill died without ever coming to a vote [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who pay at or near the minimum wage are better off, since the 50-cent increase never took effect. Workers earning the minimum wage keep the pre-1996 floor of $4.25 an hour under this bill, though Congress did enact a separate minimum wage increase in 1996.

for.name: Rep. Phil English
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to raise the minimum wage to $4.75 an hour.

for.name: 3 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, its only cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on Economic and Educational Opportunities
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee on workforce protections and never took it up; the bill received no markup or vote.

against.name: Rep. Bill Goodling
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Economic and Educational Opportunities
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled committee action on the bill, which died in subcommittee.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Allowed minimum wage legislation to sit in committee through 1995 while resisting wage increases, before a separate compromise bill passed in 1996.

against.name: President Bill Clinton
against.what_they_did: Publicly pushed Congress throughout 1995-96 to raise the minimum wage, keeping pressure on the issue while this bill stalled.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes to measure party splits; the sponsor was a Republican and its three cosponsors were Democrats, so support was bipartisan but thin.

industries.note: Restaurants are among the largest employers of minimum-wage workers, so a 50-cent increase in the wage floor directly raises their labor costs; the bill's death spared them that cost.

industries.industry: Retail and other low-wage service employers
industries.note: Retailers and other businesses paying at the $4.25 floor would have faced higher payroll costs under the bill; it never took effect.
Workers at or near the wage floor would have gained 50 cents an hour. The bill's death meant they saw no raise from this bill.
